question: A 38-year-old woman presents with nasal obstruction, anosmia, and clear rhinorrhoea for 18 months. Anterior rhinoscopy reveals pale, smooth, insensate masses bilaterally. Which feature of this presentation is most consistent with benign nasal polyps rather than a sinonasal malignancy?

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Unilateral nasal masses should raise suspicion for malignancy, inverted papilloma, or JNA — not benign polyps.

answers.text: Bilateral, pale, insensate, mobile masses with anosmia

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. Benign nasal polyps are classically bilateral, pale (oedematous), insensate (no pain on probing), and mobile. Anosmia reflects obstruction of the olfactory cleft. Unilateral or bleeding masses demand urgent rethink.
Blood-stained discharge is a red-flag feature suggesting malignancy or JNA, not simple polyps.
Bony expansion indicates an aggressive lesion such as inverted papilloma, malignancy, or mucopyocoele — not simple nasal polyps.

overallFeedback.feedback: Review the clinical features of nasal polyps. The key distinguishing features are bilaterality, pale colour, insensitivity to probing, and mobility — all reflecting eosinophilic mucosal oedema rather than a solid tumour.

Well done. The bilateral, pale, insensate character of nasal polyps with anosmia is the classic clinical picture. Any unilateral, bleeding, or bony-expanding nasal mass must be treated as malignancy until proven otherwise.
